\chapter{Telling Time}
\label{ch:ka-telling-time}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell someone the time on the hour in Kannada.}

Say \kn{ಗಂಟೆ} — hour, and also \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{} — then \kn{ಒಂದು} \kn{ಗಂಟೆ} and \kn{ಎರಡು} \kn{ಗಂಟೆ} for one and two o'clock.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gaṇṭe]{\kn{ಗಂಟೆ} — the same \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{} word as Hindi, borrowed through Prakrit}

\label{lesson:KA-C18-gante}



\begin{quote}
You've already met Hindi's \emph{ghanṭā} — \textquotedblleft{}hour,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}bell.\textquotedblright{} Kannada has the exact same word, arriving by the exact same logic.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಗಂಟೆ}} (\emph{gaṇṭe}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hour}\textquotedblright{} — and, just like Hindi, it means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{bell, gong}\textquotedblright{} just as commonly. It's related to the same Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{घण्टा}} (\emph{ghaṇṭā}, \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{}). The semantic shift is identical to Hindi's: temples, towns, and clock towers announced the hour by striking a bell, so the bell-word became the hour-word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This is a genuinely different picture from Tamil's. Kannada's \emph{gaṇṭe}, like Hindi's \emph{ghanṭā}, is a \textbf{Sanskrit-derived} \textquotedblleft{}bell $\to$ hour\textquotedblright{} word. Tamil, by contrast, most likely uses a \textbf{native Dravidian} word for exactly the same \textquotedblleft{}bell $\to$ hour\textquotedblright{} idea — a different root entirely, arrived at independently (though even specialists don't call this fully settled). So the \emph{pattern} (bell-word becomes hour-word) repeats across languages, but the \emph{word itself} splits along the familiar Sanskrit/native line (compare \emph{madhyāhna} vs. Tamil's \emph{naḷ}-based words for noon).
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: telling the time}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು} \kn{ಗಂಟೆ}.} — \textquotedblleft{}One o'clock.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ondu gaṇṭe}, \textquotedblleft{}one hour/bell\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಎರಡು} \kn{ಗಂಟೆ}.} — \textquotedblleft{}Two o'clock.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{eraḍu gaṇṭe})
\end{quote}

Kannada simply pairs the cardinal number with \emph{gaṇṭe} — no ordinal/cardinal split like Arabic's, no singular/plural verb switch like Hindi's \emph{bajnā}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}gaṇṭe\textquotedblright{} — hour, also \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}ondu gaṇṭe\textquotedblright{} — one o'clock
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}eraḍu gaṇṭe\textquotedblright{} — two o'clock
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nīru akki anna}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\kn{ಗಂಟೆ}} mean besides \textquotedblleft{}hour,\textquotedblright{} and what Sanskrit word is it related to? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Bell, gong\textquotedblright{}} — related to Sanskrit \emph{ghaṇṭā}.) Is this the same root Hindi uses for \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Yes} — Hindi's \emph{ghanṭā} is the same Sanskrit word.) Does Tamil use this same Sanskrit root for \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Most likely not} — it uses a native Dravidian word instead, arrived at independently.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ū]{\kn{ಊ} — one character, the long partner of one you already have}

\label{lesson:KA-S127-letter-uu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಉ} — what sound does it carry, and does it stand alone or ride on a consonant?

One character this time. It is the same vowel held longer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಊ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಊ}} — \emph{ū}, the long \emph{u}.

Kannada keeps \textbf{short and long as two different letters}, not as one letter with a mark on it. So the vowel you met two chapters ago has a partner:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಉ}} — \emph{u}, short. Say it and stop.
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಊ}} — \emph{ū}, long. Say it and hold it about twice as long.
\end{itemize}

Look at the shapes: \textbf{\kn{ಊ}} is \textbf{\kn{ಉ}} with an extra stroke. Kannada builds the long vowel out of the short one and repeats that habit across its vowels.

The length is not decoration. It separates words, the way \emph{ship} and \emph{sheep} are separated by nothing else.

\textbf{\kn{ಊ}} has a riding half too. You have already read it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಮೂರು}} \emph{mūru} — three
\end{itemize}

That \textbf{\kn{ೂ}} in the middle is this same long vowel, drawn as a tail on \textbf{\kn{ಮ}}. Take the consonant away and it has to stand up, and standing up it is \textbf{\kn{ಊ}}.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಊ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ಊ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two and say which is the long one
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಉ}  ·  \kn{ಊ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಊ} three times, holding the \emph{ū} long as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಮೂರು} and find the riding half of today's letter inside it
  \item \emph{Say it:} the short one, then the long one — \textquotedblleft{}u … ū\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಊ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ū}}, the long \emph{u}.) How is its shape related to \kn{ಉ}? (It is \kn{ಉ} with an added stroke.) What is its riding half, and in which word have you already read it? (\textbf{\kn{ೂ}}, in \emph{mūru}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[0]{\kn{೦} — the digit for hattu}

\label{lesson:KA-S149-digit-zero}



\begin{quote}
Before the new shape: \textbf{\kn{೯}} — which number is it?

One digit this time, and you already know its name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{೦}}
\textbf{\kn{೦}} — \textbf{0}, the digit for \textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತು}} (\emph{hattu}), \textquotedblleft{}zero\textquotedblright{}.

Zero. On its own it is nothing; behind another digit it multiplies by ten, which is how \kn{ಹತ್ತು} is written \textbf{\kn{೧೦}} — a \kn{೧} and a \kn{೦}, exactly as \emph{10} is.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{೦} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{೦} and follow its line. Copy the shape in front of you — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what you can see needs no such source.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the digits you have met, and name each one aloud
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{೧}  ·  \kn{೨}  ·  \kn{೩}  ·  \kn{೪}  ·  \kn{೫}  ·  \kn{೬}  ·  \kn{೭}  ·  \kn{೮}  ·  \kn{೯}  ·  \kn{೦}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
